The manuscript is well organized and visually clear, with many implementation hyperparameters and dataset-processing details reported.
weaknesses: There is no held-out test set: the 80/20 split is described as training/validation, guidance weights are tuned for fidelity and quality, and the reported targets and metrics are computed on that same validation set. Combined with the absence of repeated training runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests, this substantially weakens the quantitative evidence.

The principal compositional baseline is configured unfairly. With independent 0.1 dropout over six conditions, an example containing only one active condition occurs with probability 0.9*0.1^5, while the unconditional mask occurs with probability 0.1^6. The catastrophic baseline results for zero or one constraint therefore largely demonstrate an extremely imbalanced mask-training scheme. Structured mask sampling or uniformly sampled subsets would be a much stronger comparison.

The compositionality claim is not adequately tested beyond fixed nested subsets of at most six structures. Targets appear to come from coherent validation cases rather than independently mixed or conflicting attributes, and the compositional experiment reports generation-quality metrics but not per-structure target errors. Thus, arbitrary recombination and simultaneous constraint satisfaction remain insufficiently demonstrated.

Generality beyond the heart is supported almost entirely by three qualitative samples each for the aorta, spine, and knee. There are no quantitative fidelity, realism, topology, or baseline results for these datasets, so the broad cross-anatomy claims are stronger than the evidence.

The method can worsen anatomical validity. Table 8 reports higher connected-component errors under guidance than under unconditional sampling, notably for the aorta, pulmonary artery, and inferior vena cava. This is consequential for the claimed simulation use case, and filtering invalid generations does not resolve the underlying failure. The single biomechanical example also cannot establish reliable counterfactual or causal utility.

The morphological realism metrics are constructed from essentially the same mass, centroid, and covariance features optimized by the guidance loss, partially favoring the proposed method. Point-cloud metrics provide some independent support, but averaging them across labels can conceal local defects, and no expert anatomical assessment is provided.

The technical novelty is moderate: the method largely combines established loss-based diffusion guidance with classical geometric moments. Comparisons cover retrained conditional models but omit alternative training-free losses or guidance approaches, such as differentiable overlap, distance-field, bounding-box, or point-set constraints, which would better isolate the benefit of the proposed moment representation.

Reproducibility and practicality remain incomplete: code and checkpoints are not identified; manual filtering criteria, split identifiers, random seeds, sampler details, and the magnitude of the denominator-stabilizing noise are missing. Runtime and memory are also unreported despite decoding and backpropagating through a full 128^3 multi-label volume at every one of 50-100 denoising steps.

weaknesses: The algorithmic novelty is modest. The method largely combines elementary differentiable geometric moments with established loss-based diffusion guidance; the distinction from prior universal/compositional guidance and ellipsoid-based control, particularly ProtComposer, is not established strongly enough for a top-tier general AI venue.

The central compositionality claim is inadequately tested. Targets are jointly consistent moment sets drawn from individual validation cases, and experiments use a few fixed, nested label subsets. There is no evaluation of cross-patient recombination, incompatible or out-of-distribution constraints, arbitrary subsets, or conditional-fidelity scaling as more structures are constrained. Results on aorta, spine, and knee are qualitative only.

The principal compositional baseline is unfairly trained. With independent dropout probability 0.1 over six condition channels, the all-dropped configuration occurs with probability 10^-6 and a specified one-channel-only configuration with probability 9×10^-6. Its failure for zero or few constraints is therefore expected. A uniformly sampled subset curriculum is needed. Moreover, with all six constraints, the implicit baseline matches or exceeds the proposed method on most Table 1 metrics.

Parts of the evaluation are circular. Guidance directly optimizes mass, centroid, and covariance, while the reported morphological realism metrics are constructed from essentially the same moments. Point-cloud metrics are averaged over tissues and can conceal defects in the guided structure. No independent anatomical plausibility assessment, surface-quality evaluation, or expert review is provided.

Statistical evidence is weak: experiments generally use only 100–200 generated samples, report no confidence intervals, variation across sampling seeds, significance tests, or independent training runs. The same validation set supplies targets and evaluation data and appears to inform guidance-weight tuning, with no held-out test set.

Topology—the property most important for the claimed simulation use case—often worsens under guidance. In Table 8, guided samples have more extra components than unconditional samples for the aorta, pulmonary artery, inferior vena cava, and right atrium. Global moments cannot enforce connectivity or clinically important local geometry, making claims of realistic or simulation-ready anatomy too strong.

The biomechanical study is anecdotal: it uses one seed anatomy, three variants, no unguided-inpainting control, simplified material and wall assumptions, and no validation or uncertainty analysis. It therefore does not support the concluding causal claim about anatomical form and simulated function.

Reproducibility and practicality are incomplete. Important sampler, optimization, random-seed, baseline-training, manual-filtering, and stabilization details are missing; no code or trained models are identified; and runtime or memory costs are not reported despite requiring decoder and denoiser backpropagation at every one of 50–100 sampling steps. Clinical bias and safety implications of automatically segmented, manually filtered training data and topologically invalid outputs are also insufficiently discussed.

The experimental scope is appreciable: the authors examine conditioning baselines, guidance-strength sweeps, attribute ablations, multiple constrained structures, dataset scaling, reconstruction limits, extreme editing factors, and a procedural ellipsoid dataset.

The appendix is unusually candid about failure modes. In particular, the topology analysis and out-of-distribution scaling experiment reveal where guidance degrades samples rather than concealing these limitations.
The downstream finite-element example is a potentially useful bridge between controllable generative modeling and simulation workflows.
The manuscript is generally well organized, and the diagrams explain the sampling procedure effectively.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited. Geometric moments are classical differentiable statistics, and applying their losses through standard diffusion posterior or universal guidance is a straightforward combination. The paper does not adequately distinguish its contribution from closely related ellipsoid-based compositional generation, especially ProtComposer, beyond changing the application domain.

The central compositional comparison is not fair. The implicit baseline independently drops six conditioning channels with probability 0.1, making a specified one-channel condition occur with probability 9e-6 and the fully unconditional condition with probability 1e-6. The authors explicitly attribute the baseline's failure to this design. A baseline trained with balanced mask patterns or global conditioning dropout is required. Indeed, when all six conditions are present, the implicit baseline matches or outperforms the proposed method on most Table 1 metrics.

Several quality measurements are partly circular. Targets are sampled from the same validation distribution used for evaluation, while the morphological embedding is constructed from masses, centroids, and covariance eigenvalues—the same low-order quantities being explicitly optimized. Strong scores therefore do not establish realistic local anatomy, topology, or clinical plausibility.

The claimed arbitrary compositionality is not demonstrated. Experiments use fixed nested label subsets and coherent moment tuples copied from validation subjects, rather than independently recombined, conflicting, rare, or out-of-distribution constraints. Scalability is tested only up to six structures.

Topological validity is a major unresolved issue for the stated simulation use case. Table 8 shows that guidance increases connected-component errors, reaching mean extra-component counts of 1.458 for the aorta and 1.042 for the pulmonary artery. Suggesting post-hoc filtering without reporting its rejection rate, bias, or effectiveness does not support claims of realistic or simulation-ready generation.

Generality beyond the cardiac dataset is supported only by a few qualitative examples for the aorta, spine, and knee, without quantitative fidelity, topology, baseline, or expert assessments. The biomechanical evidence is likewise a single selectively successful case using an idealized RV wall and does not substantiate the broader causal or clinical claims.

Experimental rigor is insufficient for a top-tier acceptance: guidance weights are tuned and evaluated on the same validation set; there is no held-out test set; plots and tables lack confidence intervals, repeated-training variability, or significance testing; some studies use only 24 or 32 samples; and manual data-selection criteria are unspecified.

Reproducibility and practicality are incomplete. No code, exact splits, random seeds, model parameter counts, hardware, training cost, inference runtime, or memory overhead are reported; the magnitude of the denominator-stabilizing noise is omitted. Full-volume decoding and backpropagation at every one of 50–100 denoising steps may be substantially more expensive than the conditional baselines, but no cost comparison is provided.
